title: The Shannon number
hook: Chess has more possible games than there are atoms in the observable universe.
peek: In 1950 Claude Shannon estimated that chess allows about 10 to the power of 120 different games. That number dwarfs the roughly 10 to the 80 atoms in the observable universe, and it explains why no computer can solve chess by brute force.
lede: In 1950 Claude Shannon, the founder of information theory, wrote a paper on how a computer might play chess. To show why it could not simply check every option, he made a rough estimate. Around a thousand possibilities for each pair of moves, over a typical game of 40 moves, gives about 10 to the power of 120 possible games. It became known as the Shannon number.

bullets.text: The observable universe is usually estimated to hold around 10 to the 80 atoms. Shannon's number is larger by a factor of 10 to the 40, a gap too big to picture.
The number of legal positions on a chessboard is far smaller, with modern estimates around 10 to the 44. The huge count of games comes from the many routes between those positions.

Since checking everything was hopeless, Shannon sketched two ways forward: search every move to a limited depth, or look only at promising moves, more like a human. Chess programs still use versions of both ideas.
When IBM's Deep Blue beat Garry Kasparov in 1997, it searched huge numbers of positions per second but only a sliver of the whole game. Nobody yet knows whether perfect play ends in a win or a draw.
